questions.stem: In the sentence "Because the road was flooded, the lorry took the longer route", the group of words *Because the road was flooded* is
questions.explanation: The group has a subject, *the road*, and a finite verb, *was*, so it is a clause. But *Because* makes it dependent on the rest of the sentence — read it alone and it leaves the listener waiting — so it is subordinate. The main clause is *the lorry took the longer route*, which can stand by itself.

distractorRationale.a: A main clause makes complete sense alone, which this one does not because of *Because*
distractorRationale.c: It contains a finite verb, so it cannot be a phrase
distractorRationale.d: It does not name a thing; it gives a reason

questions.stem: In the sentence "The bridge that the contractor repaired collapsed last week", the clause *that the contractor repaired* is

options.text: a noun clause acting as subject

questions.explanation: The clause tells us which bridge collapsed, so it describes the noun *bridge* and is doing an adjective's job. Adjectival clauses, also called relative clauses, are introduced by who, whom, whose, which, that, when or where and always sit next to the noun they describe.

distractorRationale.a: The subject of the sentence is the noun phrase *The bridge that the contractor repaired*, not this clause alone
distractorRationale.c: *Last week* is the time expression; this clause answers 'which one', not 'when'
distractorRationale.d: It cannot stand alone, so it is subordinate

questions.stem: In the sentence "What the witness said surprised the whole court", the clause *What the witness said* functions as
questions.explanation: Ask "what surprised the court?" and the answer is the whole clause, so it occupies the subject slot and is therefore a noun clause acting as subject. The substitution test confirms it: replace the clause with *It* and you get "It surprised the whole court", a complete sentence.

distractorRationale.b: *The whole court* is the object; the clause comes before the verb
distractorRationale.c: It does not tell us which court; it names the thing that caused the surprise
distractorRationale.d: An adverbial clause of reason would begin with *because* or *since*

questions.stem: In the sentence "The farmers began to plant as soon as the first rains fell", the clause *as soon as the first rains fell* is an adverbial clause of
questions.explanation: The clause answers the question "when did the farmers begin to plant?", and any adverbial clause that answers *when* is a clause of time. The subordinator *as soon as* belongs to the time family along with when, while, before, after, until and since.

distractorRationale.a: A clause of reason answers 'why' and begins with because, since or as
distractorRationale.c: A clause of condition begins with if or unless and states what must be true first
distractorRationale.d: A clause of purpose begins with so that or in order that

questions.stem: In the sentence "Everyone knows that the examination has been postponed", the clause *that the examination has been postponed* functions as
questions.explanation: Ask "everyone knows what?" and the whole clause answers, so it is a noun clause serving as the direct object of *knows*. Replace it with *it* — "Everyone knows it" — and the structure is unchanged, which confirms the clause is filling a noun slot.

distractorRationale.a: It does not tell us which people are meant; it names what is known
distractorRationale.c: A result clause would begin with *so that* and describe a consequence
distractorRationale.d: *Everyone* is the subject, and it comes before the verb

questions.stem: In the sentence "Although the fees were increased, enrolment rose sharply", the subordinate clause expresses
questions.explanation: *Although* admits a fact that works against what follows, so the clause expresses concession — often described as contrast. The sense is 'the fees went up, and yet enrolment still rose'. Other concessive subordinators are though, even though, while and whereas.

distractorRationale.b: A reason clause would say the fee increase caused the rise, which is the opposite of the meaning here
distractorRationale.c: A clause of manner answers 'how' and begins with *as* or *as if*
distractorRationale.d: A clause of place answers 'where' and begins with *where* or *wherever*

questions.stem: In the sentence "Abeokuta is the town where my grandmother was born", the clause *where my grandmother was born* is

options.text: a noun clause acting as complement

questions.explanation: Although it begins with *where*, the clause does not tell us where anything happened in the sentence as a whole; it tells us which town is meant. Because it describes the noun *town*, it is adjectival. The lesson is that the introducing word alone never settles the classification — the job the clause does settles it.

distractorRationale.a: The commonest error here: students see *where* and assume place. An adverbial of place would modify a verb, as in 'She sat where the shade was thickest'
distractorRationale.c: *The town where my grandmother was born* as a whole is the complement, but the relative clause alone only describes *town*
distractorRationale.d: Nothing in the clause answers 'when'

questions.stem: A main clause can stand alone as a complete sentence.
questions.explanation: True. A main or independent clause has a subject and a finite verb and expresses a complete thought, so it needs nothing else: "The lorry took the longer route". A subordinate clause has the same subject and finite verb but is opened by a subordinator such as *because* or *although*, which leaves it dependent.

questions.stem: In the sentence "The panel awarded the contract to whoever submitted the lowest bid", the clause *whoever submitted the lowest bid* functions as
questions.explanation: The preposition *to* needs an object, and the whole clause supplies it, so the clause is a noun clause serving as the object of a preposition. Note that *whoever* stays in the subjective form because it is the subject of *submitted* inside the clause — the preposition governs the clause as a unit, not the single word after it.

distractorRationale.a: It does not tell us which contract was awarded
distractorRationale.c: It names a recipient rather than describing how the award was made
distractorRationale.d: *The panel* is the subject of the sentence

questions.stem: In the sentence "That the accused acted in self-defence was clear to the judge", the clause *That the accused acted in self-defence* is a noun clause functioning as
questions.explanation: The finite verb of the whole sentence is *was*, and asking "what was clear?" gives the whole *That...* clause, so it fills the subject slot. You could rewrite the sentence as "It was clear to the judge that the accused acted in self-defence", where the introductory *It* stands in for the clause — proof that the clause is the real subject.

distractorRationale.b: *Clear* is the complement of *was*, describing the subject
distractorRationale.c: *Acted* is intransitive here and takes no object; *in self-defence* is an adverbial phrase
distractorRationale.d: It gives no reason, and *that* is not a subordinator of reason

questions.stem: In the sentence 'When the sun sets, the sky turns orange', the clause *When the sun sets* is classified as which type?
questions.explanation: The clause 'When the sun sets' provides information about the time of the main action, which is turning orange. Therefore, it functions as an adverbial clause.

distractorRationale.a: A noun clause acts as a subject or object, which is not the case here.
distractorRationale.b: An adjectival clause modifies a noun, but this clause modifies the verb instead.
distractorRationale.d: A main clause can stand alone, but this clause cannot.
